Online fraud is becoming more expensive, and stopping it is only one of the objectives enterprise leaders have to manage.

Consumers reported losing $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025, up from just over $12 billion a year earlier, the Federal Trade Commission told Congress in March 2026.

Over the same year, the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center logged more than one million complaints and nearly $21 billion in losses, and devoted a section of its annual report to AI-enabled schemes for the first time.

For merchants and money-movement businesses, every defensive decision creates a second risk: declining a legitimate transaction, adding unnecessary verification, delaying a refund or pushing a valuable customer out of the funnel. Fraud, payments, and customer experience (CX) leaders increasingly need to accurately isolate a very small population of bad actors to remove friction for everyone else.

​In a webinar series produced with Riskified, Emerj examines how fraud is shifting from individual transactions to identities and behavioral patterns, and why the wrong decision now costs far more than a chargeback. The series included conversations with Danielle Dzbanek, Senior Director of Analytics at Riskified, Jeff Otto, Chief Marketing Officer at Riskified, Robert Rose, Senior Director of Customer Experience at Adobe, and Debjit Saha, VP of Engineering and Product, Risk and Compliance at MoneyGram.​

Across ecommerce, software and remittances, the guests make it clear that modernizing fraud prevention without sacrificing growth rests on four practices:​

Guest: Jeff Otto, Chief Marketing Officer at Riskified

​Expertise: AI-Powered Risk Intelligence, B2B Marketing Strategy, Fintech Marketing, Financial Services Technology

Brief Recognition: Jeff Otto serves as CMO at Riskified, leading global marketing for an AI-powered ecommerce risk intelligence platform serving enterprise brands. Previously, he led marketing at Marqeta and spent more than seven years at Salesforce building and scaling industry and product marketing across financial services, healthcare, and enterprise technology, following earlier leadership experience within Morgan Stanley’s technology and data division. Otto earned an MBA in Finance from Texas McCombs School of Business, where he was a Venture Fellow and Dean’s Award recipient.

Guest: Danielle Dzbanek, Senior Director of Analytics at Riskified

​Expertise: Data Analytics, Fraud & Risk Analytics, Marketing Analytics, Data Strategy

Brief Recognition: Danielle Dzbanek has built her career leading analytics teams and data strategy initiatives across digital advertising and fraud prevention. At Riskified, she progressed from analytics team lead to Senior Director of Analytics, overseeing analytics efforts across the Americas and supporting data-driven decision-making for risk and commerce. Prior to Riskified, she spent more than five years at MediaMath in progressively senior analytics roles and was recognized with the 2019 IAB Data Rockstar Award for innovation and impact in the data industry. She holds a BBA from Emory University with a focus on Finance, Marketing, and Analytic Consulting.

Guest: Robert Rose, Senior Director of Customer Experience at Adobe

​Expertise: Customer Success, Technical Support Operations, Knowledge Management, Service Transformation

Brief Recognition: Robert Rose led enterprise paid support for Adobe’s Creativity and Productivity Solutions business, where he created and scaled the company’s global paid support program for Digital Media solutions. Across a career spanning leadership roles at Adobe, NICE, EMC, and Symantec, Rose has led large-scale support and customer success transformations, including global technical support organizations, knowledge management systems, and customer experience initiatives. Beyond industry leadership, he served as Adjunct Faculty at Utah Valley University, where he received a Teacher of the Year award, and holds a Bachelor of Science in Business from the University of Phoenix.

Guest: Debjit Saha, VP of Engineering and Product, Risk and Compliance at MoneyGram

​Expertise: Financial Crime Technology, Fraud and Risk Engineering, Product Management, AI and Machine Learning

Brief Recognition: Debjit Saha is VP of Engineering and Product, Risk and Compliance at MoneyGram, where he builds data- and AI-driven controls for fraud, compliance, and payments decisioning. He previously advised large global financial institutions as a senior management consultant at EY. He holds a Master of Business Administration from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.

When Riskified analyzes merchant populations, Jeff Otto says, identities associated with losses can represent roughly 20 basis points of the customer base, which he compares to a few drops of poison in a lake. Those individuals rarely look that small inside transactional systems, because one person may operate dozens of accounts. For Otto, this reframes the question: not whether a transaction or account looks fraudulent, but whether seemingly separate accounts belong to the same person.

​In her episode, Danielle Dzbanek describes how fraud rings exploit the same blind spot across merchants. Attackers once studied one site, found its vulnerabilities, and concentrated there. Today, she explains, fraudsters care about the goods, not which store they come from. A technique that works at one merchant gets carried to the next, and the next. Because each merchant sees only its own piece of the attack, none can recognize the pattern alone.

​One account-takeover ring Riskified tracked in ticketing started with small test purchases, escalated once something worked, and then repeated the pattern at six merchants over several months. In her view, no business can understand modern fraud using only its own data:

​“If you’re sitting in your silo, it’s hard to know what’s going on out there. You need that network effect now. You can’t work in isolation anymore. You can’t look at your own population and try to stop fraud there.”

— Danielle Dzbanek, Senior Director of Analytics at Riskified

​Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, is Otto’s clearest example of what clustering identities reveals. Its losses to refund abuse ran to roughly $4 million, Otto says, and traced back to just 600 people, who had created tens of thousands of accounts to run refund-as-a-service schemes.

Otto describes the mechanism as identity resolution: linking physical addresses, emails, phone numbers, IP addresses, devices, and payment credentials until what a customer data platform shows as 50 different people resolves into one person, operating what he calls a garage scam center. Once those actors are isolated, he explains, stronger controls can apply to them without imposing the same cost on the rest of the customer base.

​Network-level information also changes how teams should treat first-time customers. Someone who has never purchased from a particular site, Dzbanek points out, may still carry observable history through shipping addresses, IPs, devices and buying patterns elsewhere, so a new customer is not necessarily an unknown one.

​Dzbanek also notes that off-the-shelf tools can now alter IDs, fake selfies and clone voices, which makes verification at sign-up less definitive. Debjit Saha describes MoneyGram’s response as a layered identity model that adds device, IP and behavioral information to traditional know-your-customer (KYC) checks.
